newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Killings on rise in Rwanda, UN rights monitors say.
newsitem.headline: Killings on rise in Rwanda, UN rights monitors say.

text.p: The United Nations human rights operation in Rwanda said on Friday security there had deteriorated sharply in January, when at least 424 people were reportedly killed -- the highest monthly figure in a year.
In a report, the U.N. operation also said seven expatriates had been killed in Rwanda since the start of 1997, including four of its international staff in an ambush earlier this month.

The rise in violence since the return late last year of one million Rwandan Hutus from exile in Zaire and Tanzania, has prompted the U.N. to cut the number of rights' monitors from the current 131 to 104, U.N. sources said.
"We have decided to bring down our presence in Rwanda. We are reducing the numbers," a U.N. source told a news briefing.

Since their colleagues were killed and operations suspended in most of the country, about 20 of the 131 monitors have elected to quit at month-end and will not be replaced due to security fears, he said. The rest remain confined to Kigali and were unable to monitor abuses country-wide in February.

"The human rights situation has drastically deteriorated since the beginning of January, in particularly in the four prefectures bordering Zaire," said the report by the U.N. human rights field operation in Rwanda (HRFOR), issued in Geneva.

"The HRFOR is concerned by the increase in killings and attacks against genocide survivors and persons associated with them. HRFOR is also seriously concerned about the significant increase in killings of unarmed civilians during military operations in January and a number of public extrajudicial executions in December and January," it added.
The U.N. operation received reports of the killings of at least 424 people in 55 incidents. "This represents the highest number of reported killings since the beginning of 1996."
At least 163 of the 424 killings last month were reportedly "the responsibility of the state, including members of the RPA", according to the report.
It had no information on the identities of the perpetrators repsonsible for the remaining 194 killings reported in January, including 43 carried out by men "wearing military uniforms".
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals after the genocide of an estimated 800,000 minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates before Tutsi-led rebels seized power in Kigali.

The government blames the new wave of violence on Hutu former troops and extremist militiamen who sneaked back into the country among the other refugees. Targeted by the Hutu militiamen are genocide witnesses who could testify in court, as well as Tutsi civilians.
